K. W. Jeter initially attracted my attention because I was angry about typical characterizations of cyberpunk. In short, I felt that Gibson and Sterling got too much credit for their contributions to cyberpunk, and I was looking to find some other author that I could credit as the true creator of cyberpunk.

My first foray into this was Jeter's book Dr. Adder. This book astounded me. It had been written in the 1970s, but it had not been published until the 1980s. If it had found a publisher before Neuromancer had, perhaps Jeter would be more famous than Gibson today. Dr. Adder is the best story I have found from Jeter, and if you only have time to read one Jeter book, start with Dr. Adder. It might seem ever so slightly unpolished, but it delivers amazingly vivid world-building. The titular character, Dr. Adder is a magnificent bastard of an antihero who is much more worldly-wise than the protagonist. You might decide that you hate him, but you will have to admit that he is an interesting guy to read about. The protagonist is much less of a badass, but he is a tough, competent survivor with the courage to face overwhelming odds. The plot has multiple conflicts that attacked the protagonist from all angles. The story is sprawling and picaresque but engaging and comprehensible. Reading this book was like taking a psychedelic drug and having an entirely new experience.

The second Jeter book I read was Infernal Devices. This book was more polished but less visionary. The protagonist was not at all competent and could only survive by the skin of his teeth. The antiheroic characters were antagonists, with considerably less appeal than Dr. Adder. The plot has essentially one well-coordinated set of conflicts that attack the protagonist from just one angle. The story was as neatly tied together as an Agatha Christie murder mystery. The atmosphere was consistent and convincing, but it did not deliver much world-building. Reading this book was like consuming a large, well-cooked meal, with dessert and hot cocoa afterward.

The third Jeter book I read was The Glass Hammer. The protagonist initially seemed only slightly weak, but in some ways it could be argued that he was extremely underpowered relative to the challenges of the story. The protagonist has a friend who is much more worldly-wise, but that friend is not a powerful badass like Dr. Adder. There are some supporting characters who are highly competent, but they are not charismatic antiheroes. The world-building was competent but Jeter spent a lot of effort on some abstract themes that do not seem to come together meaningfully. The plot has some shocking twists. Reading this book is like getting drunk with the television on and getting confused about how much of your emotional turmoil is internal and how much is inspired by the television. I enjoyed this book the least of all three of these books.
